title: Backtracking
summary: Backtracking builds an answer one choice at a time and undoes each choice after exploring it. It walks a tree of decisions, and pruning cuts off branches that cannot lead to a valid answer.
idea: explore(state): if it is complete, record a copy. Otherwise, for each allowed choice: choose it, explore, then un-choose it. Stop a branch early when it can no longer succeed.

signals.see: The question asks for all subsets, permutations, combinations, arrangements or partitions.
signals.think: The output itself is exponential, so no shortcut exists. Generate each answer with choose, explore, un-choose.

signals.see: Place items under constraints: queens, Sudoku digits, words on a board.
signals.think: Try each option for the next slot, check the constraints, and back up as soon as one fails rather than at the end.

signals.see: Inputs are small, often n ≤ 10 to 20, and the answer is a list of lists.
signals.think: Small limits are a hint that an exponential search is expected. Spend your effort on pruning.

phrasings: List every way to pick dishes from a menu so the bill comes to exactly the budget.
Place n guards on an n × n board so no two share a row, column or diagonal.
Return every valid arrangement of n pairs of brackets.

picture.title: Generate and filter versus choose, explore, un-choose
picture.alt: On the left, every possible combination is built in full and only checked at the end, so hopeless branches are expanded completely. On the right, a single path list grows by one choice, the search goes deeper, and the choice is popped on return; a branch is cut as soon as it cannot reach the target.
picture.caption: One shared path, undone on the way back, plus early pruning.

code.py:
def pick_sum(nums, target):
    a, out, path = sorted(nums), [], []  #@init
    def explore(start, left):
        if left == 0: out.append(path[:]); return  #@found
        for i in range(start, len(a)):
            if a[i] > left: break  #@prune
            path.append(a[i])  #@choose
            explore(i + 1, left - a[i])  #@explore
            path.pop()  #@unchoose
    explore(0, target)
    return out  #@done

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 4 different whole numbers from 1 to 20, and a target from 1 to 40. Each number can be used at most once.

oneLiner: explore(start): if complete, save a copy; for each choice: if it can fit, push it, explore, pop it

exercise.prompt: Return every way to choose k different numbers from 1 to n, each list in increasing order, with the lists in lexicographic order. For example, combos(4, 2) starts [1, 2], [1, 3], [1, 4], [2, 3]. The starter never un-chooses, so its path keeps growing.
hints: Keep one path list. Add a number, recurse with only larger numbers allowed, then remove it.
Record a copy of path when it holds k numbers; the list itself keeps changing.
Prune: if fewer numbers remain than slots left to fill, stop the loop.

complexity.why: There are 2ⁿ subsets (or n! permutations) and copying each answer costs O(n). Pruning cuts the work in practice but not the worst case. The recursion and path are O(n) deep.

mistakes: Appending path itself instead of a copy, so every saved answer ends up as the same final list.
Forgetting to un-choose, so choices from one branch leak into the next.
Producing duplicates when the input repeats a value. Sort it and skip a value equal to the previous one at the same depth.
Pruning with a test that only works on sorted input without sorting first.

quiz.question: Why record path[:] (a copy) instead of path?
choices: path keeps changing as the search continues, so every saved reference would end up the same
quiz.explain: All saved references point at one list, which is empty by the end.

quiz.question: Numbers are sorted, and a[i] is already bigger than what is left of the target. What can you do?
choices: Break: every later number is bigger too
quiz.explain: Sorting turns one failed check into a cut of the whole rest of the loop.

quiz.question: How do subsets and permutations differ in the loop?
choices: Subsets start the loop after the last choice; permutations loop over every unused item
quiz.explain: Order matters for permutations, so any unused item may come next; a used set or swap tracks them.

interviewTip: Draw the first two levels of the decision tree before coding. It shows the interviewer what one call does, where you prune and what you record.
